summary: Every box and stage of the task-queue page is stated in design.md; the one soft spot is 'exactly one worker', which the design qualifies as not a hard mutex. The page is a thin overview: it omits the direct task-failure path, the collision check on automated ingestion, dependency and priority ordering, and stale-lease recovery.

code.overview: The design describes a queue shared across projects and stored as GitHub Issues. What is built is a queue for one repository: a local SQLite store (.agent/queue/queue.db) with a Markdown view (queue.md), driven by scripts/queue.ts, queue-model.ts, queue-io.ts, queue-db.ts, queue-claim.ts and queue-worktrees.ts. Built: manual adding, dependency ordering, claiming under a lock, a lease clock, worktree per task, running the validate command, retry then failed. Not built anywhere in this repo: the GitHub Issues store and its labels, assign-and-verify claiming, cross-project targeting, the push trigger, GitHub Action workers, automated and assistant-proposed ingestion with the collision check, the high/default priority tiers, the proposed and reconciling states, and any merge-back or reconciliation code (merging is done by the agent and the root from skills/queue.md). Two built behaviours contradict the design: an expired lease blocks dispatch instead of returning the task to pending, and an agent is refused when it tries to add a task on its own.

refs.anchor: if (!title) { console.error('usage: queue add "<title>" [--parent <id> | --requested "<human words>"] [flags]'); return 1; }
refs.title: queue add: the one built ingestion path
refs.explain: The command joins its arguments into a title and refuses an empty one. It asks taskOrigin whether this caller may add a task. It then appends the task (or puts it first with --top), saves, logs, and prints the new id plus a drain marker if the task can run now.
refs.why: This is manual ingestion as built: one task per call, written by whoever runs the command. There is no alignment loop or slicer in code; the caller supplies deps, files and validate as flags.

refs.anchor: if (parent && !q.tasks.some(t => t.id === parent)) return { ok: false, error: `queue add: --parent ${parent} is not a task in this queue` };
refs.title: taskOrigin: agents may not add tasks on their own
refs.explain: It reads the --parent and --requested flags. A named parent must be an existing task. With neither flag, a human is allowed, but a session that carries an agent environment marker is refused with an explanation. With a flag, the origin is recorded on the task as a tag and a note.
refs.why: This is the opposite of the design's automated ingestion: the code blocks agent-created tasks unless a human asked for them. No watcher, cron or telemetry source feeds the queue.

refs.anchor: contracts    TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]' CHECK (json_valid(contracts) AND json_type(contracts) = 'array'),
refs.title: SCHEMA: the queue store is a local SQLite file
refs.explain: The store has a meta table for config, a tasks table and a views table that remembers the hash of the rendered queue.md. A task row holds id, position, status, dependencies, files, validate command, failures, owner, branch, worktree and start time. Status can only be pending, active, done or failed, and position is unique.
refs.why: This takes the place of the GitHub Issues store in the design. It has no repo, priority, assignee, heartbeat or deferrals column, and no proposed or reconciling status, so those parts of the task schema cannot be stored.

refs.anchor: throw new Error(`queue: lock ${path} remained held for ${LOCK_WAIT_MS}ms; `
refs.title: acquire: one lock file makes every queue command atomic
refs.explain: It tries to create the lock file beside the store in exclusive mode and writes its pid and time into it. If the file already exists it checks whether the holder process is dead and, if so, takes over. Otherwise it waits 20 ms and tries again, and after 60 seconds it throws.
refs.why: Every CLI command runs inside this lock, so two workers on the same machine cannot both claim one task. This replaces the design's assign, re-read and verify on a GitHub issue; it does not work across machines.

refs.anchor: /** A pending task is eligible only when it isn't held and every dependency is done. */
refs.title: isEligible: the dependency gate
refs.explain: A task is eligible when it is pending, not held, allowed by the current delivery cycle, and every task it depends on is done. deadlocked lists pending tasks that depend on a failed task, which can never become eligible.
refs.why: This is the design's rule that a task never starts before its dependencies complete, and that a failure only strands its dependents. Order among eligible tasks is the line order of the queue; the two priority tiers are not built.

refs.title: claim: lease a task to a worker
refs.explain: It refuses a task that is not pending, is held, or is blocked by an unfinished delivery cycle. It takes the worker name from --worker or makes one from the process id. In one save it marks the task active, records the owner and start time, and links a branch if --branch was given.
refs.why: This is the claim step. It is safe because the caller already holds the queue lock, not because of a verify-after-write.

refs.anchor: console.log(`queue: DELIVERY PENDING — ${q.config.deliveryTask}; finish its PR/merge cycle and fresh branch, then advance`);
refs.title: dispatchGate: an expired lease stops dispatch
refs.explain: Before any task is handed out, it resumes a paused queue whose pause time has passed, and reports a stopped or paused queue. It then looks for active tasks whose start time is older than leaseMinutes. If any exist it prints OWNERSHIP CONFLICT and returns exit code 6 without changing them. It also blocks while a finished task still waits for its merge to be acknowledged.
refs.why: The design says a stale lease returns the task to pending for another worker. The code deliberately does not: it stops and asks for the owner to be resolved, so a slow worker is never doubled up.

refs.anchor: /** Stable prefix a Monitor / cron / agent keys on to (re)start a stalled drain. */
refs.title: drainSignal: tell a poller that work is waiting
refs.explain: It returns nothing when the queue is stopped or any task is active. Otherwise it counts eligible tasks and, if there are any, returns the line "queue: DRAIN-WANTED <n> pending". The queue signal command prints that line, and add, set and top append it to their output.
refs.why: This is the built form of distribution: something polls the local queue and wakes a worker when the marker appears. The push path (an issue or label event firing a worker) does not exist.

refs.anchor: ? `queue: IDLE — ${stuck.length} task(s) blocked by a failed dependency: ${stuck.map(x => x.id).join(', ')}`
refs.title: tick: a worker pulls the next task
refs.explain: It runs the dispatch gate and returns its exit code if blocked. It picks an already active task if there is one, else the first eligible task from the top. With nothing to do it prints IDLE, naming tasks stuck behind a failed dependency, and exits 3. Otherwise it marks the task active and prints the task block with the done and fail commands to run after.
refs.why: This is the pull a Phase 1 worker makes. The agent then does the work itself; the script does not start an agent.

refs.anchor: + `Delivery mode: ${q.config.deliveryMode}. Read skills/queue.md: per-task requires root PR, real local and hosted validation, authorized merge and fresh branch before advance; exit 7 is pending delivery, not drained. `
refs.title: queue loop: print the routine a Claude session runs
refs.explain: It prints a /loop instruction for the current queue. A paused queue gets a slow poll. Otherwise the text tells the session to arm a monitor that polls queue signal, then repeat tick (or ready, for parallel batch mode) while the exit code is 0, stop on idle, and stop and report on an ownership conflict.
refs.why: This is how the worker substrate is built: a text instruction for a live agent session, with exit codes to steer it. Phase 2, a GitHub Action that drains the queue on a schedule, has no workflow in .github/workflows.

refs.anchor: + `First step in the lane: \`git merge --ff-only ${base}\` (a reused branch may be stale); stop if it cannot fast-forward. `
refs.title: worktree add: an isolated checkout per task
refs.explain: It takes the base from the integrationBranch setting, or the current branch if that is blank. It creates a git worktree at .agent/queue/wt/<id> on a new branch queue/<id> cut from the base, or reuses the branch if it exists. It records the branch and worktree path on the task and prints what the lane should do next, including that the root does the integration.
refs.why: This is the worktree-per-task rule, in the same repository as the queue. Checking out a different target repo from a project label is not built.

refs.title: done: run validate, then complete
refs.explain: If the task has a validate command it releases the lock, runs the command in the task's worktree, and reloads the queue; a task that changed meanwhile is refused. A failing command records a failure and exits 1. A pass marks the task done, then moves it and any done tasks nothing still depends on into the archive.
refs.why: This is the validation gate before a task counts as completed. It checks the task branch only; it does not merge and does not re-run validation on the merged result.

refs.anchor: const tasks = terminal ? q.tasks.map(t => (t.id === id ? updated : t)) : [...rest, updated];
refs.title: recordFailure: retry, then failed
refs.explain: It adds one to the task's failure count and stores the reason as its note. Below maxFailures the task goes back to pending at the end of the line with its owner and worktree link cleared. At maxFailures it becomes failed and keeps its place.
refs.why: The design marks a task failed on the first failure and deletes its worktree. The code retries up to maxFailures (default 3) and only clears the worktree link; removing the worktree is a separate command.

refs.anchor: console.error('advance: requires selected completed task, no active claims, --pr <merged-pr-url> and --branch <fresh-working-branch>');
refs.title: advance: the root says the merge happened
refs.explain: It requires that the named task is the one awaiting delivery, is done and accepted, that no task is active, and that a pull request URL and a fresh branch name were given. It then clears the delivery latch so the next task can be dispatched, and logs the PR and branch.
refs.why: This is the only code at the merge-back step, and it is an attestation: the script does not merge, check the PR, or detect conflicts. Until it runs, dispatchGate holds the next task back.

promptOnly.what: the target repo is whichever repository the task names.

Not built: /queue ingest with its alignment loop and slicer, automated watcher/cron/telemetry ingestion with the context-collision check and deferral count, and assistant proposals with a proposed state; an agent breaks work into tasks by hand from skills/queue.md and adds them one at a time.

Not built: the GitHub Issues store with status/priority/project labels, assign-then-verify claiming, a heartbeat that returns a stale task to pending, the push trigger, cross-project sharing and the high/default priority tiers; the store is one repository's local SQLite file.
Phase 1 is an agent session following the printed /loop text and skills/queue.md; Phase 2 GitHub Action worker crons are not built (the only queue workflow, agent-loop.yml, runs tests).

Not built: checking out a target repo from a project label, the merge-back into the integration branch, the reconciling state and the automatic high-priority reconciliation task; the agent applies changes, and the root merges and resolves conflicts by hand under skills/queue.md.
